differential: Neonatal sepsis
Early-onset sepsis commonly presents with feeding difficulties and behavioral changes in the first days of life.
Hypoglycemia
Newborns are susceptible to low blood sugar, which manifests as poor feeding, lethargy, and abnormal behavior.
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (kernicterus)
Day 3 is peak time for physiologic jaundice, and severe cases can cause lethargy and poor feeding.
Inborn errors of metabolism
Metabolic disorders often present after initial feeding with lethargy, poor feeding, and neurological symptoms in the first week of life.
Congenital heart disease
Undetected cardiac anomalies can present with feeding difficulties and lethargy as pulmonary pressures change in early neonatal period.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out any diagnoses.

differential: Inborn error of metabolism (urea cycle defect, organic acidemia, or maple syrup urine disease)
Lethargy, seizures, and hyperventilation in a 3-day-old after initial normal period suggests metabolic decompensation with accumulation of toxic metabolites.
Neonatal sepsis (bacterial meningitis)
Early-onset or late-onset sepsis can present with lethargy, seizures, and respiratory abnormalities in the first week of life.
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Seizures and lethargy may indicate delayed manifestation of perinatal hypoxia despite reportedly uncomplicated delivery.
Hypoglycemia
Newborns are vulnerable to hypoglycemia which can cause lethargy, seizures, and compensatory hyperventilation.
Intracranial hemorrhage
Spontaneous or birth-related hemorrhage can present with seizures and altered consciousness even after apparently normal vaginal delivery.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses, as multiple serious conditions can present similarly in neonates.

differential: Urea cycle disorder (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency)
Hyperammonemia with elevated glutamine, decreased BUN, and cerebral edema in a neonate are classic findings of impaired urea cycle function.
Carbamyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
This urea cycle defect presents identically with severe hyperammonemia, low BUN, and neurological symptoms in the first days of life.
Citrullinemia (argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency)
This urea cycle disorder causes neonatal hyperammonemia with elevated glutamine and similar clinical presentation, though typically citrulline levels would be markedly elevated.
Organic acidemia (propionic or methylmalonic acidemia)
These can present with hyperammonemia and neurological symptoms in neonates, though typically also feature metabolic acidosis and ketosis.
Transient hyperammonemia of the newborn
This idiopathic condition causes severe hyperammonemia in the first days of life with similar symptoms, though it is less common and a diagnosis of exclusion.
eliminated: Neonatal sepsis
While sepsis can cause lethargy and seizures, it would not typically cause the specific pattern of hyperammonemia with decreased BUN and elevated glutamine.
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
The uncomplicated vaginal delivery and specific metabolic derangements (hyperammonemia with low BUN) make this unlikely.

differential: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
Genetic testing confirms CPS1 gene mutation, and clinical presentation with neonatal hyperammonemia, seizures, and cerebral edema is pathognomonic.
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Presents similarly with neonatal hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine, though genetic testing confirmed CPS1 rather than OTC mutation.
N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency
Clinically indistinguishable from CPS1 deficiency with hyperammonemia and low BUN, but genetic testing excludes this diagnosis.
Citrullinemia type I
Part of urea cycle disorders with similar neonatal presentation, but would show elevated citrulline levels and genetic testing confirmed CPS1 deficiency instead.
Argininosuccinic aciduria
Another urea cycle disorder presenting with neonatal hyperammonemia, but biochemical profile and confirmed CPS1 mutation distinguish this case.
eliminated: Sepsis
Would not explain the specific metabolic derangements (hyperammonemia, low BUN, elevated glutamine) or the confirmed CPS1 gene mutation.
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Vaginal delivery without complications and specific metabolic pattern with genetic confirmation rule this out.
Inborn errors of organic acid metabolism
Would typically show metabolic acidosis and abnormal organic acids rather than isolated hyperammonemia with low BUN.
Transient hyperammonemia of the newborn
Would resolve spontaneously and would not have an underlying genetic mutation in CPS1.

differential: Neonatal sepsis
A 3-day-old newborn with feeding difficulties and behavioral changes is at risk for early-onset sepsis, which commonly presents with nonspecific symptoms including poor feeding and lethargy.
Neonatal hypoglycemia
Feeding difficulties in the first days of life can lead to or result from hypoglycemia, which presents with jitteriness, lethargy, and feeding problems.
Neonatal jaundice with kernicterus risk
Day 3 of life is peak time for physiologic jaundice, and severe hyperbilirubinemia can cause lethargy, poor feeding, and abnormal behavior.
Inborn errors of metabolism
Metabolic disorders often present in the first week of life with poor feeding, lethargy, and unusual behavior as toxic metabolites accumulate.
Neonatal hypocalcemia
Early neonatal hypocalcemia (first 72 hours) can present with jitteriness, irritability, and feeding difficulties.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses.

differential: Congenital TORCH infection (toxoplasmosis, CMV, rubella, HSV)
Hepatosplenomegaly and neonatal seizures are classic presentations of intrauterine infections affecting the CNS and reticuloendothelial system.
Neonatal sepsis with meningitis
Early-onset bacterial infection can present with seizures, feeding difficulties, and splenomegaly in the first days of life.
Inborn error of metabolism (galactosemia or organic acidemia)
Metabolic disorders can present with feeding intolerance, seizures, and hepatosplenomegaly within the first days after milk feeding initiation.
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Birth-related hypoxia can cause neonatal seizures and feeding difficulties, though splenomegaly would be unusual.
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (ABO or Rh incompatibility)
Significant hemolysis can cause splenomegaly, and severe hyperbilirubinemia with kernicterus can lead to seizures.
eliminated: Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus
The presence of splenomegaly and true seizures excludes this benign condition.
Physiologic feeding difficulties
Splenomegaly and seizures indicate pathologic process beyond normal newborn adjustment.

differential: Urea cycle disorder (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency)
Hyperammonemia with elevated glutamine, low BUN, and cerebral edema in a neonate are classic findings of defective urea cycle enzyme function.
Carbonic anhydrase VA deficiency
This rare disorder causes hyperammonemia with low BUN due to impaired hepatic ureagenesis, though less common than primary urea cycle defects.
Organic acidemia (propionic or methylmalonic acidemia)
These can cause hyperammonemia and seizures in neonates, though typically associated with metabolic acidosis and ketonuria not mentioned here.
Citrin deficiency (citrullinemia type II)
This aspartate-glutamate carrier deficiency causes neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with hyperammonemia and hepatomegaly/splenomegaly.
Transient hyperammonemia of the newborn
A self-limited condition causing severe hyperammonemia in the first days of life with cerebral edema, though typically without the specific pattern of elevated glutamine and low BUN.
eliminated: Neonatal sepsis
The infant is afebrile and the specific metabolic pattern (hyperammonemia, elevated glutamine, low BUN) points to a metabolic rather than infectious etiology.
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
The uncomplicated vaginal delivery and specific metabolic derangements make this unlikely.
